title: The attack chain behind the v1.107.0 LiteLLM release
excerpt: How a master key committed to a public repository in May led to three stolen GitHub tokens and the compromised litellm v1.107.0 release, step by step.
content_html:
On October 21, our release pipeline published a compromised litellm==1.107.0 to PyPI and to our container registries. The incident post covers the affected artifacts and what to do if you ran them. We have completed our investigation into the actions taken by the threat actor, and can confidently assert the timeline and sequence of events that led to the publication of the malicious v1.107.0 release.

We posted regular status updates during our investigation yesterday reflecting the scenario to the best of our knowledge as the investigation proceeded. The investigation was ongoing, and some assumptions and beliefs in those updates were later proven to be inaccurate or incomplete. This post is the canonical source of truth.

Narrative​

On May 27, 2026, a configuration file was committed to the public LiteLLM-Labs/lite-harness repository which inadvertently contained the master key to a deployment of the LiteLLM Agent Platform, an open source tool we use for orchestrating agents. The error was quickly identified, the commit force-pushed over, and we identified the exposed keys as requiring revocation. However, key revocation did not occur for the master key.

GitHub Owner Access​

LiteLLM Agent Platform was an experimental project for self-hosted cloud agents to file PRs to GitHub repositories. In order to create PRs, the system was configured with a GitHub authentication token. The token in question was not associated with a service account and was not scoped down. The key used was a GitHub CLI OAuth token associated with our GitHub organization owner's account.

On October 10th, the threat actor used this key to gain access to our LiteLLM Agent Platform and extracted this GitHub CLI OAuth token. From this point onwards, the threat actor had owner-level access to all repositories in our GitHub. GitHub CLI tokens are post-2fa and not subject to GitHub's "super-user" 2fa reauth flows associated with sensitive organization or repository actions.

Exfiltrating additional tokens​

Using the access provided by the Github CLI OAuth token, the threat actor began to perform additional credential exfiltration actions. They authored commits into branches on internal repositories to execute workflows designed to exfiltrate any tokens and secrets configured to be available to CI in our repositories. In so doing, they acquired similar GitHub CLI Oauth tokens associated with two engineers with maintainer privileges.

They also acquired tokens to several other internal systems. Reviewing the actor's activity on these other systems shows attempts to identify and exfiltrate additional keys and tokens, with a primary focus on upstream inference API tokens.

While we have traced out all tokens we believe the threat actor could have accessed, we are revoking every token associated with every internal system and vendor platform. This incident has provided a strong illustration of the risks associated with failing to rotate a potentially exposed key.

Building and Signing the Malicious Release​

Having access to multiple GitHub identities, the threat actor was now in a position to be able to make changes to our repositories without being overly noisy, concealing changes within proper-seeming proposals and approvals. The threat actor began by attempting to subvert our project releaser repository to have it pull the package from a different (malicious) repository. They were unable to get approval to merge due to heavily restricted approvals on the repository. As such, they opted to for the noisier approach of using the org owner's token to bypass and disable restrictions on the repository, pushing the change.

In typical operation, building and publishing a release requires being kicked off by an authorized engineer and being approved by a special account locked to a physical device in our office. This restriction was relaxed earlier this week to accommodate the temporary push for more frequent releases and bugfix backports, allowing any two engineers to trigger and approve a release. As such, the threat actor used one of the tokens to trigger the release (after having repointed the deployer to their malicious repository), and another to approve it.

It is worth noting, however, that armed with a token belonging to an organization owner, the threat actor could very well have relaxed this restriction (or removed it entirely) themselves. However, we believe they used the separate tokens in order to evade detection by way of noisy audit logs.

Aftermath and Containent​

The malicious releases were published to our public registries at around 4:40 AM PDT (11:40 UTC). We became aware of the malicious releases shortly before 6 AM (13:00 UTC) and immediately began the process to remove them. The PyPi releases were frozen by 6:23 AM PDT (13:23 UTC). The Docker images took us a bit longer as we worked to wake the inviduals with access to our Docker registry, and were removed by 7:20 AM PDT (14:20 UTC).

In response, at the beginning of our investigation, we took the following temporary mitigation approaches:

  • We immediately locked our public registries to prevent additional images from being published.
  • As soon as we suspected GitHub accounts were compromised, we removed all members from our GitHub organization, with the exception of a single specific account temporarily promoted to owner which we could be confident was not affected.
  • We began operating in a mode which assumes that every possible token, key, or authenticator belonging to our organization was exfiltrated.

As investigations began to shed light on the scope and details of the attack, we were able to begin laying out a roadmap necessary for secure account and process reinstatement.

At this point, we are confident in our ability to safely issue a release by EOD today, providing our users with a fix for removing the eMudhra certificate authority from our trust store. We understand it has been frustrating that we have been slow to issue a release to remediate this high-profile issue. We will only issue releases when we can be confident in their safety.

Process Improvements​

We know many of you want to hear what we’ve learned and what we’re changing. We’ll share that next week.

Annotated Events​

Step 1: the master key returns a GitHub token (October 10, 21:13 to 21:28)​

From 69.48.229.143, the attacker called the Agent Platform API with the master key.

  1. Between 21:13 and 21:28 the attacker made a series of authenticated requests to the API.
  2. At 21:27:10 a request to GET /api/v1/managed_agents/agents?limit=100 returned the configuration of every managed agent.
  3. That response contained the GitHub CLI OAuth token of one of our two GitHub organization owners.

Step 2: a throwaway branch exfiltrates the CI secrets of BerriAI/litellm (October 10, 22:11)​

With the owner's token, the attacker turned a repository's own CI into the exfiltration channel.

  1. The attacker pushed commit b69bc36 on a branch named ci-tmp-a351cc to BerriAI/litellm.
  2. Its workflow run started at 22:11:45 and posted six repository secrets to an attacker-controlled webhook.site endpoint.
  3. One of them, GH_TOKEN, held the GitHub CLI OAuth token of a second maintainer.
  4. At 22:14:14 the attacker deleted the run with the owner's token.

The GitHub audit log records a hash of the token behind each action, and the hash of GH_TOKEN matches the token that approved the release in step 5.

Step 3: Further exfiltrations (October 10, 22:12; October 12 12:08-12:30)​

  1. Twenty-four seconds after step 2, commit 78d968b on branch ci-tmp-be33e9 in BerriAI/litellm-auto ran a workflow that posted RELEASE_PLEASE_TOKEN to the same endpoint.
  2. That secret held the GitHub CLI OAuth token of a third maintainer.
  3. The run was deleted at 22:14:31.

Its token hash matches the token that deleted the release runs in step 6.

In addition, the attacker ran a second round of exfiltrations two days later across a variety of private repos. This includes commit 1a6e3c1, which exfiltrated some minimally sensitive secrets and minimally funded provider keys used in our CI testing. See the details in the Socket report.

The additional secrets were not involved in the path taken towards the poisoned artifacts, and were resolved by rotating involved tokens and auditing security logs for access.

Step 4: the release workflow is pointed at a fork (October 21, 10:08 to 11:08)​

Our releases are built by workflows in the private BerriAI/project-releaser repository. From 199.91.221.39, the attacker changed where those workflows take their source from.

  1. The attacker authored commit 9cf97e9 ("ci: release from a fork source repository") as the organization owner. It let the release workflow build from a source repository other than BerriAI/litellm.
  2. At 10:08:29 a push of that commit to main with the second maintainer's token was rejected by branch protection, which requires a pull request, two passing checks, and approval from the codeowner for this workflow.
  3. At 10:08:34 the attacker disables branch protections and then force-pushes with the owner's token.
  4. At 10:46:39 the attacker dispatched the staging workflow at 9cf97e9, as the owner, with the source set to the lookalike Berri-AI/litellm at commit 20535d8f.
  5. The staging run finished at 11:08:09 and the production release pipeline started at 11:08:53.

Commit 20535d8f exists only on the attacker's fork, but it opens at github.com/BerriAI/litellm/commit/20535d8f because GitHub serves a fork's commits through the repository it was forked from.

Step 5: the production gate is approved with a stolen token (11:11:18)​

  1. The second maintainer's token approved the production environment gate of the release run, from 199.91.221.39.
  2. The pipeline signed and published v1.107.0 built from the fork commit.
  3. Seven PyPI wheels went out between 11:39:51 and 11:40:13.
  4. The Docker Hub and GHCR images went out at 11:46:56.

Step 6: the run records are deleted (11:53)​

  1. The third maintainer's token deleted the production run record at 11:53:49.
  2. It deleted the staging run record at 11:54:01.

Both deletions removed the workflow logs from the repository.

Step 7: the workflow history is force-pushed clean (12:09 to 12:24)​

With the owner's token, again by overriding branch protection, the attacker removed the change from the visible history.

  1. At 12:09:32 the attacker committed a revert of 9cf97e9, commit 285fbdc5, and pushed it at 12:09:38.
  2. At 12:24:52 they force-pushed main back to d687b69, the commit before the change, overriding GitHub's force-push block as well.

main then showed neither the change nor the revert. Both commits are still retrievable by SHA, and the organization audit log recorded each override.

Acknowledgements​

We would like to thank LidorMachluf for their service to the open source community by catching the malicious release within 20 minutes of publication, maintaining a thorough writeup of the issue, and keeping it up to date with ongoing analysis and information.

We would also like to thank Karlo Zanki and the Socket Threat Research team for sharing their investigation with us and coordinating on disclosure of their findings.

Additionally, we want to give a big thanks to Asritha Bodepudi and Evan Sultanik at Trail of Bits, who have been assisting us with internal security audits as part of Patch the Planet and were also very helpful in addressing, investigating, and communicating about this incident.

blocks.html_en: On May 27, 2026, a configuration file was committed to the public LiteLLM-Labs/lite-harness repository which inadvertently contained the master key to a deployment of the LiteLLM Agent Platform, an open source tool we use for orchestrating agents. blocks.html_en: GitHub Owner Access​

sentences.en: GitHub Owner Access​

blocks.html_en: LiteLLM Agent Platform was an experimental project for self-hosted cloud agents to file PRs to GitHub repositories. In order to create PRs, the system was configured with a GitHub authentication token. The token in question was not associated with a service account and was not scoped down. The key used was a GitHub CLI OAuth token associated with our GitHub organization owner's account.

sentences.en: LiteLLM Agent Platform was an experimental project for self-hosted cloud agents to file PRs to GitHub repositories.
In order to create PRs, the system was configured with a GitHub authentication token.
The token in question was not associated with a service account and was not scoped down.
The key used was a GitHub CLI OAuth token associated with our GitHub organization owner's account.

blocks.html_en: On October 10th, the threat actor used this key to gain access to our LiteLLM Agent Platform and extracted this GitHub CLI OAuth token. From this point onwards, the threat actor had owner-level access to all repositories in our GitHub. GitHub CLI tokens are post-2fa and not subject to GitHub's "super-user" 2fa reauth flows associated with sensitive organization or repository actions.

sentences.en: Exfiltrating additional tokens​

blocks.html_en: Using the access provided by the Github CLI OAuth token, the threat actor began to perform additional credential exfiltration actions. They authored commits into branches on internal repositories to execute workflows designed to exfiltrate any tokens and secrets configured to be available to CI in our repositories. In so doing, they acquired similar GitHub CLI Oauth tokens associated with two engineers with maintainer privileges.

In so doing, they acquired similar GitHub CLI Oauth tokens associated with two engineers with maintainer privileges.

blocks.html_en: They also acquired tokens to several other internal systems. Reviewing the actor's activity on these other systems shows attempts to identify and exfiltrate additional keys and tokens, with a primary focus on upstream inference API tokens.

blocks.html_en: Having access to multiple GitHub identities, the threat actor was now in a position to be able to make changes to our repositories without being overly noisy, concealing changes within proper-seeming proposals and approvals. The threat actor began by attempting to subvert our project releaser repository to have it pull the package from a different (malicious) repository. They were unable to get approval to merge due to heavily restricted approvals on the repository. As such, they opted to for the noisier approach of using the org owner's token to bypass and disable restrictions on the repository, pushing the change.

blocks.html_en: In typical operation, building and publishing a release requires being kicked off by an authorized engineer and being approved by a special account locked to a physical device in our office. This restriction was relaxed earlier this week to accommodate the temporary push for more frequent releases and bugfix backports, allowing any two engineers to trigger and approve a release. As such, the threat actor used one of the tokens to trigger the release (after having repointed the deployer to their malicious repository), and another to approve it.

content_html_zh:
On October 21, our release pipeline published a compromised litellm==1.107.0 to PyPI and to our container registries. The incident post covers the affected artifacts and what to do if you ran them. We have completed our investigation into the actions taken by the threat actor, and can confidently assert the timeline and sequence of events that led to the publication of the malicious v1.107.0 release.

We posted regular status updates during our investigation yesterday reflecting the scenario to the best of our knowledge as the investigation proceeded. The investigation was ongoing, and some assumptions and beliefs in those updates were later proven to be inaccurate or incomplete. This post is the canonical source of truth.

Narrative​

On May 27, 2026, a configuration file was committed to the public LiteLLM-Labs/lite-harness repository which inadvertently contained the master key to a deployment of the LiteLLM Agent Platform, an open source tool we use for orchestrating agents. The error was quickly identified, the commit force-pushed over, and we identified the exposed keys as requiring revocation. However, key revocation did not occur for the master key.

GitHub Owner Access​

LiteLLM Agent Platform was an experimental project for self-hosted cloud agents to file PRs to GitHub repositories. In order to create PRs, the system was configured with a GitHub authentication token. The token in question was not associated with a service account and was not scoped down. The key used was a GitHub CLI OAuth token associated with our GitHub organization owner's account.

On October 10th, the threat actor used this key to gain access to our LiteLLM Agent Platform and extracted this GitHub CLI OAuth token. From this point onwards, the threat actor had owner-level access to all repositories in our GitHub. GitHub CLI tokens are post-2fa and not subject to GitHub's "super-user" 2fa reauth flows associated with sensitive organization or repository actions.

Exfiltrating additional tokens​

Using the access provided by the Github CLI OAuth token, the threat actor began to perform additional credential exfiltration actions. They authored commits into branches on internal repositories to execute workflows designed to exfiltrate any tokens and secrets configured to be available to CI in our repositories. In so doing, they acquired similar GitHub CLI Oauth tokens associated with two engineers with maintainer privileges.

They also acquired tokens to several other internal systems. Reviewing the actor's activity on these other systems shows attempts to identify and exfiltrate additional keys and tokens, with a primary focus on upstream inference API tokens.

While we have traced out all tokens we believe the threat actor could have accessed, we are revoking every token associated with every internal system and vendor platform. This incident has provided a strong illustration of the risks associated with failing to rotate a potentially exposed key.

Building and Signing the Malicious Release​

Having access to multiple GitHub identities, the threat actor was now in a position to be able to make changes to our repositories without being overly noisy, concealing changes within proper-seeming proposals and approvals. The threat actor began by attempting to subvert our project releaser repository to have it pull the package from a different (malicious) repository. They were unable to get approval to merge due to heavily restricted approvals on the repository. As such, they opted to for the noisier approach of using the org owner's token to bypass and disable restrictions on the repository, pushing the change.

In typical operation, building and publishing a release requires being kicked off by an authorized engineer and being approved by a special account locked to a physical device in our office. This restriction was relaxed earlier this week to accommodate the temporary push for more frequent releases and bugfix backports, allowing any two engineers to trigger and approve a release. As such, the threat actor used one of the tokens to trigger the release (after having repointed the deployer to their malicious repository), and another to approve it.

It is worth noting, however, that armed with a token belonging to an organization owner, the threat actor could very well have relaxed this restriction (or removed it entirely) themselves. However, we believe they used the separate tokens in order to evade detection by way of noisy audit logs.

Aftermath and Containent​

The malicious releases were published to our public registries at around 4:40 AM PDT (11:40 UTC). We became aware of the malicious releases shortly before 6 AM (13:00 UTC) and immediately began the process to remove them. The PyPi releases were frozen by 6:23 AM PDT (13:23 UTC). The Docker images took us a bit longer as we worked to wake the inviduals with access to our Docker registry, and were removed by 7:20 AM PDT (14:20 UTC).

In response, at the beginning of our investigation, we took the following temporary mitigation approaches:

  • We immediately locked our public registries to prevent additional images from being published.
  • As soon as we suspected GitHub accounts were compromised, we removed all members from our GitHub organization, with the exception of a single specific account temporarily promoted to owner which we could be confident was not affected.
  • We began operating in a mode which assumes that every possible token, key, or authenticator belonging to our organization was exfiltrated.

As investigations began to shed light on the scope and details of the attack, we were able to begin laying out a roadmap necessary for secure account and process reinstatement.

At this point, we are confident in our ability to safely issue a release by EOD today, providing our users with a fix for removing the eMudhra certificate authority from our trust store. We understand it has been frustrating that we have been slow to issue a release to remediate this high-profile issue. We will only issue releases when we can be confident in their safety.

Process Improvements​

We know many of you want to hear what we’ve learned and what we’re changing. We’ll share that next week.

Annotated Events​

Step 1: the master key returns a GitHub token (October 10, 21:13 to 21:28)​

From 69.48.229.143, the attacker called the Agent Platform API with the master key.

  1. Between 21:13 and 21:28 the attacker made a series of authenticated requests to the API.
  2. At 21:27:10 a request to GET /api/v1/managed_agents/agents?limit=100 returned the configuration of every managed agent.
  3. That response contained the GitHub CLI OAuth token of one of our two GitHub organization owners.

Step 2: a throwaway branch exfiltrates the CI secrets of BerriAI/litellm (October 10, 22:11)​

With the owner's token, the attacker turned a repository's own CI into the exfiltration channel.

  1. The attacker pushed commit b69bc36 on a branch named ci-tmp-a351cc to BerriAI/litellm.
  2. Its workflow run started at 22:11:45 and posted six repository secrets to an attacker-controlled webhook.site endpoint.
  3. One of them, GH_TOKEN, held the GitHub CLI OAuth token of a second maintainer.
  4. At 22:14:14 the attacker deleted the run with the owner's token.

The GitHub audit log records a hash of the token behind each action, and the hash of GH_TOKEN matches the token that approved the release in step 5.

Step 3: Further exfiltrations (October 10, 22:12; October 12 12:08-12:30)​

  1. Twenty-four seconds after step 2, commit 78d968b on branch ci-tmp-be33e9 in BerriAI/litellm-auto ran a workflow that posted RELEASE_PLEASE_TOKEN to the same endpoint.
  2. That secret held the GitHub CLI OAuth token of a third maintainer.
  3. The run was deleted at 22:14:31.

Its token hash matches the token that deleted the release runs in step 6.

In addition, the attacker ran a second round of exfiltrations two days later across a variety of private repos. This includes commit 1a6e3c1, which exfiltrated some minimally sensitive secrets and minimally funded provider keys used in our CI testing. See the details in the Socket report.

The additional secrets were not involved in the path taken towards the poisoned artifacts, and were resolved by rotating involved tokens and auditing security logs for access.

Step 4: the release workflow is pointed at a fork (October 21, 10:08 to 11:08)​

Our releases are built by workflows in the private BerriAI/project-releaser repository. From 199.91.221.39, the attacker changed where those workflows take their source from.

  1. The attacker authored commit 9cf97e9 ("ci: release from a fork source repository") as the organization owner. It let the release workflow build from a source repository other than BerriAI/litellm.
  2. At 10:08:29 a push of that commit to main with the second maintainer's token was rejected by branch protection, which requires a pull request, two passing checks, and approval from the codeowner for this workflow.
  3. At 10:08:34 the attacker disables branch protections and then force-pushes with the owner's token.
  4. At 10:46:39 the attacker dispatched the staging workflow at 9cf97e9, as the owner, with the source set to the lookalike Berri-AI/litellm at commit 20535d8f.
  5. The staging run finished at 11:08:09 and the production release pipeline started at 11:08:53.

Commit 20535d8f exists only on the attacker's fork, but it opens at github.com/BerriAI/litellm/commit/20535d8f because GitHub serves a fork's commits through the repository it was forked from.

Step 5: the production gate is approved with a stolen token (11:11:18)​

  1. The second maintainer's token approved the production environment gate of the release run, from 199.91.221.39.
  2. The pipeline signed and published v1.107.0 built from the fork commit.
  3. Seven PyPI wheels went out between 11:39:51 and 11:40:13.
  4. The Docker Hub and GHCR images went out at 11:46:56.

Step 6: the run records are deleted (11:53)​

  1. The third maintainer's token deleted the production run record at 11:53:49.
  2. It deleted the staging run record at 11:54:01.

Both deletions removed the workflow logs from the repository.

Step 7: the workflow history is force-pushed clean (12:09 to 12:24)​

With the owner's token, again by overriding branch protection, the attacker removed the change from the visible history.

  1. At 12:09:32 the attacker committed a revert of 9cf97e9, commit 285fbdc5, and pushed it at 12:09:38.
  2. At 12:24:52 they force-pushed main back to d687b69, the commit before the change, overriding GitHub's force-push block as well.

main then showed neither the change nor the revert. Both commits are still retrievable by SHA, and the organization audit log recorded each override.

致谢​

We would like to thank LidorMachluf for their service to the open source community by catching the malicious release within 20 minutes of publication, maintaining a thorough writeup of the issue, and keeping it up to date with ongoing analysis and information.

We would also like to thank Karlo Zanki and the Socket Threat Research team for sharing their investigation with us and coordinating on disclosure of their findings.

Additionally, we want to give a big thanks to Asritha Bodepudi and Evan Sultanik at Trail of Bits, who have been assisting us with internal security audits as part of Patch the Planet and were also very helpful in addressing, investigating, and communicating about this incident.
